newsitem.title: USA: Republicans to voice discontent with Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Republicans to voice discontent with Gingrich.

text.p: A band of disgruntled conservative House Republicans planned to gather Tuesday to express discontent with House Speaker Newt Gingrich's handling of the recent disaster aid showdown with President Clinton.

An aide to one of the conservative members said the meeting was a chance for members to discuss how the party will handle coming fights with the Clinton administration over tax cuts and annual spending bills.
Another aide said Republicans were concerned about "leadership drift," and the whether they were compromising too much with the White House and Democrats on core party issues.
House leaders were not invited and neither Gingrich nor his deputies were scheduled to attend.

But aides to Republican leaders played down the importance of the invitation-only meeting and said Gingrich's hold on the speakership was secure. They also dismissed as unimportant an anonymous letter circulating on Capitol Hill which called upon Republicans to challenge Gingrich's leadership.
Nevertheless, Gingrich's top deputy, Majority Leader Richard Armey, pointedly declined to give the speaker a whole-hearted endorsement in response to several questions at his weekly news conference.
Armey, a Texas Republican, was asked flat out whether he thought the Speaker was doing an effective job. "Well, have a nice day now," was his only response before he walked out.

In a written statement Armey later defended his actions, saying he had not been asked during the briefing. "Since no one asked, I assumed it was perfectly clear that the leadership continues to be a cohesive team."

Gingrich's press office commented only that Armey obviously ran out of time at his news conference, and a close aide to the speaker said he did not view the lawmaker's remarks as signalling any real break between the two.
Armey confirmed that a group of House conservatives have called a meeting to re-appraise their agenda and consider how to "move it along."
"I applaud that kind of effort," he said, calling it a "healthy thing." But he said he had not had any talks with fellow conservatives or with rank and file House members about Gingrich's leadership.

Many of the more conservative Republicans, particularly those who first came to power as part of the 1995 Republican revolution, have been upset that the party has not continued to press to reduce the size and cost of government, an aide said. This had been one of the party's central missions when it gained control of the House in the 1994 election.

This group was particularly dismayed when Congress last week sent the president a disaster aid bill exactly as he had requested to end a veto showdown. Provisions they had fought for -- to prevent a government shutdown this fall and stop the use of statistical sampling in the 2000 census -- were dropped by congressional leaders.
"We pretty much gave in to everything he wanted and gained nothing in return," the aide said.

The disaster relief legislation had proved a political disaster for the party. When Clinton vetoed the first version, sending it back with instructions to remove the offending provisions, Republicans took the blame for delay in aid reaching the flooded Midwestern states.
No author came forward to claim the anonymous letter which cited Gingrich's "blunders" during the 1995 budget battles which left the party bruised by two unpopular government shutdowns.

While the letter asked for a vote of confidence in the Republican leadership, such a negative vote by the party conference would not automatically result in a recall but would be politically damaging.
